_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Serbia covering medieval Serbian Empire (Stefan Dušan 14th century), Battle of Kosovo 1389 (defeat to Ottomans, national mythology), Ottoman rule (1459-1804), Serbian Revolution 1804-35 (Karađorđe, Miloš Obrenović), Kingdom of Serbia, WWI (Black Hand, Sarajevo assassination 1914 triggered war, 1.1M Serbian dead ~28% of population), Kingdom of Yugoslavia 1918-41, WWII (Axis occupation, Partisans vs Chetniks), communist Yugoslavia (Tito 1945-80), Milošević era (1989-2000), Yugoslav Wars (Slovenia/Croatia/Bosnia 1991-95, Kosovo 1998-99), NATO bombing 1999, EU/Kosovo issues.

religion.note: Serbian Orthodox Church (autocephalous since 1219, Patriarch, central to Serbian identity); church-state close (Milošević used church nationalism); Kosovo/Metohija sacred to Serbs (1389 Battle, medieval monasteries UNESCO); Islam in Sandz̈ak region (Bosniak); Catholic Vojvodina (Hungarian, Croatian)

ethnic_groups.name: Serbian
ethnic_groups.notes: South Slavic; Orthodox; Cyrillic alphabet (national identity marker); Kosovo 1389 central to national mythology ('Vidovdan', St. Vitus Day); Greater Serbia idea (19th century irredentism, Milošević revived); diaspora (1990s wars emigration ~1M, Australia, Austria, Germany, Switzerland)

ethnic_groups.name: Hungarian
ethnic_groups.notes: Vojvodina (~250k, ~13% of Vojvodina); Trianon legacy; bilingual municipalities; minority rights; autonomy demands (low-level)

ethnic_groups.name: Roma
ethnic_groups.notes: Official 2.1%, estimated 5-8% (~500k); marginalised; extreme poverty; discrimination; Mahala settlements

ethnic_groups.name: Bosniak
ethnic_groups.notes: Sandz̈ak region (Novi Pazar, 80%+ Bosniak); Muslim Slavs; Bosnian Patriotic Party; ties to Bosnia; some separatist sentiment

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Croatian (Vojvodina, 0.8%), Slovak (Vojvodina, 0.7%), Romanian/Vlach (eastern Serbia), Albanian (Preševo Valley 2%, former Kosovo ~15% pre-1999 now <1% after war/ethnic cleansing), Montenegrin, Macedonian, Bunjevci, Gorani; Jewish (pre-WWII ~80k, ~80% killed, now ~2k); German (Danube Swabians, mostly expelled post-WWII)

independence.from: Serbia and Montenegro (State Union dissolved; historical independence: 1878 from Ottoman Empire, Congress of Berlin)

country_profile.notes_unique: Battle of Kosovo 1389 (Serbian defeat by Ottomans, Prince Lazar martyred, Vidovdan/St. Vitus Day June 28, central to national mythology, 'Kosovo is the heart of Serbia'); Sarajevo assassination 1914 (Gavrilo Princip, Black Hand, killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand, triggered WWI, 1.1M Serbians died ~28% of population, highest % loss of any nation); Yugoslav Wars (1991-99, Milošević Greater Serbia project, Slovenia/Croatia/Bosnia wars, Srebrenica genocide July 1995, 8,000+ Bosniak men/boys murdered, Kosovo war 1998-99, ethnic cleansing, NATO bombing March-June 1999, 78 days); Milošević (1989-2000, nationalist demagogue, 'all Serbs in one state', wars destroyed Yugoslavia, 200k+ dead across wars, ICTY trial for war crimes/genocide, died in Hague 2006 before verdict); Kosovo (Serbian province, 90%+ Albanian, 1999 war, UN administration, 2008 independence declaration, Serbia never recognised, 'Kosovo is Serbia' official policy, Brussels dialogue); Republika Srpska (Bosnian Serb entity, Dayton Accords, close ties); EU candidate but Russia ties complicate (Vucic balancing act, Serbian-Russian Orthodox brotherhood, Kosovo non-recognition, EU sanctions on Russia not joined); Nikola Tesla (ethnic Serb born Austrian Empire/Croatia, claimed by Serbia); Exit Festival (Novi Sad, largest music festival in Balkans); Belgrade (historically 'White City', Ottoman/Habsburg wars ~140 times, bombed in WWII+1999)

current_leader.name: Aleksandar Vučić
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: SNS (Serbian Progressive Party); former ultranationalist (Radical Party, Milošević minister 1998-2000, 'kill one Serb, kill 100 Muslims' speech 1995); rebranded as pro-EU but balances Russia/China; authoritarian consolidation (controls media, opposition weak, election irregularities); Kosovo talks (Berlin Process, Brussels dialogue, no breakthrough); dominates Serbian politics since 2012; previously PM 2014-17

prime_minister.name: Milos Vučević
prime_minister.title: Prime Minister
prime_minister.notes: SNS; Vučić loyalist; former Defence Minister, mayor of Belgrade; coalition government; technocrat implementation of Vučić policy

former_leaders.name: Boris Tadić
former_leaders.notes: DS (Democratic Party); pro-EU; arrested Radovan Karadžić (Bosnian Serb war crimes); Kosovo independence 2008 (Serbia rejected); moderate; defeated by Nikolić/SNS

former_leaders.name: Vojislav Koštunica
former_leaders.notes: DOS/DSS; defeated Milošević 2000 (Bulldozer Revolution); extradited him to Hague (reluctantly); nationalist but democratic; Kosovo independent under his PM (opposed)

former_leaders.name: Slobodan Milošević
former_leaders.notes: Socialist Party; nationalist demagogue; ignited Yugoslav Wars; 'all Serbs in one state'; Kosovo/Croatia/Bosnia wars; Srebrenica genocide (complicity); NATO bombing 1999; Bulldozer Revolution October 2000 (ousted); arrested 2001; ICTY trial (war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide charges); died 2006 in Hague custody (heart attack); polarises Serbs (monster vs defender)

former_leaders.name: Josip Broz Tito
former_leaders.notes: Communist dictator of Yugoslavia; Partisan WWII hero; broke with Stalin 1948; Non-Aligned Movement founder; balanced Yugoslav ethnicities ('brotherhood and unity'); repressed nationalism; died 1980; Yugoslavia held together by his authority; collapse begun after death

910.name: Vinča Culture & Prehistory
910.description: The Vinča culture (c. 5500–4500 BCE), centred near modern Belgrade, was one of the most sophisticated Neolithic cultures in Europe, producing the enigmatic Vinča symbols that some scholars consider a proto-writing system.

sub_clusters.name: Vinča Neolithic Civilisation
sub_clusters.description: The Vinča culture's large settlements, advanced metallurgy (earliest known copper smelting in Europe), the Vinča symbols, and the culture's influence across southeastern Europe.
key_events: Vinča culture flourishes with proto-urban settlements (c. 5500–4500 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Bronze & Iron Age Tribes
sub_clusters.description: The succession of cultures from the Vinča period through Bronze Age and Iron Age, the emergence of Illyrian, Thracian, and Celtic (Scordisci) tribal groups in the Serbian lands.

910.name: Roman Serbia & Constantine the Great
910.description: The Roman provinces of Moesia and Pannonia encompassed modern Serbia. The city of Naissus (Niš) gave birth to Emperor Constantine the Great, and Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) served as one of four capitals of the Tetrarchy.

sub_clusters.name: Celtic Scordisci & Roman Conquest
sub_clusters.description: The Celtic Scordisci confederation at Singidunum (Belgrade), Roman conquest of Moesia and Pannonia, and the integration of the region into the empire's Danubian limes.

sub_clusters.name: Constantine the Great & Naissus
sub_clusters.description: The birth of Constantine at Naissus (Niš) in 272 CE, Sirmium as an imperial capital, the region as a birthplace of numerous Roman emperors (Constantius, Jovian, Gratian), and the barbarian invasions that destroyed Roman urban life.
key_events: Constantine the Great born at Naissus (Niš) (272 CE)
Sirmium serves as one of four Tetrarchic capitals (c. 293 CE)

920.name: Serbian Principalities & Nemanjić Dynasty
920.description: South Slavic settlement created Serbian principalities that oscillated between Byzantine and Bulgarian influence. The Nemanjić dynasty unified Serbia, created the autocephalous Serbian Church, and under Stefan Dušan built an empire stretching from the Danube to the Aegean.

sub_clusters.name: Early Serbian Principalities
sub_clusters.description: Slavic settlement, the Christianisation of Serbia under Byzantine influence, the first Serbian principalities (Raška, Duklja), and the struggle for independence from Byzantine and Bulgarian overlordship.

sub_clusters.name: Nemanjić Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Stefan Nemanja's founding of the dynasty, Saint Sava's establishment of the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church (1219), the coronation of Stefan as king, and the flourishing of Serbian medieval culture and monasteries (Studenica, Sopoćani).
key_events: Saint Sava establishes the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church (1219)

sub_clusters.name: Stefan Dušan's Serbian Empire
sub_clusters.description: Stefan Dušan's conquests creating a vast empire, his coronation as Emperor of Serbs and Greeks (1346), Dušan's Code (Zakonik), and the rapid fragmentation after his death leading to the Battle of Maritsa (1371).
key_events: Stefan Dušan crowned Emperor; promulgates Dušan's Code (1346)

930.name: Battle of Kosovo & Ottoman Conquest
930.description: The Battle of Kosovo (1389) became the central event of Serbian national mythology, even though Serbia survived as a vassal state for decades afterward. The fall of Smederevo in 1459 ended medieval Serbian statehood.

sub_clusters.name: Battle of Kosovo (1389)
sub_clusters.description: The epic clash between Prince Lazar's coalition and Sultan Murad I's forces on the Field of Blackbirds (Vidovdan, 28 June 1389), the death of both commanders, and the battle's transformation into the foundational myth of Serbian identity.
key_events: Battle of Kosovo – Prince Lazar and Sultan Murad I both killed (28 June 1389)

sub_clusters.name: Serbian Despotate & Fall of Smederevo
sub_clusters.description: The Serbian Despotate under Stefan Lazarević and Đurađ Branković, the construction of Smederevo fortress, and the final Ottoman conquest of Serbia in 1459.
key_events: Fall of Smederevo – end of medieval Serbian state (1459)

930.name: Ottoman Serbia – Five Centuries of Rule
930.description: Serbia endured over three centuries of Ottoman rule. The Serbian Orthodox Church preserved national identity, while major uprisings (1594, the Great Serb Migration of 1690) shaped the demographic and cultural landscape.

sub_clusters.name: Early Ottoman Rule & Serbian Resistance
sub_clusters.description: Integration into the Ottoman system, the role of the Serbian Patriarchate of Peć in preserving identity, and the Banat uprising (1594) during which the Ottomans burned the relics of Saint Sava.
key_events: Ottomans burn the relics of Saint Sava in retaliation for revolt (1594)

sub_clusters.name: Great Serb Migrations & Austrian Frontier
sub_clusters.description: The Great Serb Migration (1690) led by Patriarch Arsenije III into Habsburg territory, the establishment of the Vojvodina Serbian community, the Military Frontier, and the decay of Ottoman authority setting the stage for revolution.

940.name: Serbian Revolution & Kingdom
940.description: The Serbian Revolution (1804–17) was among the earliest national uprisings in the Ottoman Empire. Serbia gained autonomy, then full independence (1878), becoming a kingdom and regional power whose rivalry with Austria-Hungary would trigger World War I.

sub_clusters.name: First & Second Serbian Uprisings
sub_clusters.description: Karađorđe's First Serbian Uprising (1804), the brutal Ottoman reconquest (1813), Miloš Obrenović's Second Uprising (1815), and the recognition of Serbian autonomy (1830).
key_events: Karađorđe launches the First Serbian Uprising (14 Feb 1804)
Miloš Obrenović's Second Uprising secures autonomy (1815)

sub_clusters.name: Independence & Kingdom of Serbia
sub_clusters.description: Full independence at the Congress of Berlin (1878), the Obrenović-Karađorđević dynasty rivalry, Milan I's kingdom, and the 1903 May Coup installing the Karađorđević dynasty.

sub_clusters.name: Balkan Wars & Road to World War I
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's victories in the Balkan Wars (1912–13) doubling its territory, the annexation crisis with Austria-Hungary over Bosnia, and the escalating tensions leading to the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
key_events: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo triggers WWI (28 June 1914)

950.name: Serbia in the World Wars
950.description: Serbia suffered proportionally the highest casualties of any nation in World War I. In WWII, occupied Serbia experienced the Axis puppet state, the Holocaust, and a devastating civil war between Chetniks and Partisans.

sub_clusters.name: WWI – Serbia's Calvary
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's initial victories (Battle of Cer, Kolubara), the catastrophic retreat through Albania, the Salonika Front, and the ultimate liberation—with Serbia losing around a quarter of its population.
key_events: Serbian army's epic retreat through Albania (winter 1915–16)

sub_clusters.name: Interwar Kingdom of Yugoslavia
sub_clusters.description: The creation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (1918), renamed Yugoslavia (1929), Serbian political dominance, King Alexander's dictatorship, and his assassination in Marseille (1934).

sub_clusters.name: WWII – Occupation & Civil War
sub_clusters.description: The Axis invasion and dismemberment of Yugoslavia, the Nedić puppet regime, the Holocaust of Serbian Jews and Roma, the Chetnik-Partisan civil war, and Tito's victory.
key_events: Bombing of Belgrade; Axis invasion of Yugoslavia (6 April 1941)

950.name: SR Serbia in Socialist Yugoslavia
950.description: Serbia was the largest republic in Tito's Yugoslavia, containing the autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. After Tito's death, the rise of Serbian nationalism under Slobodan Milošević triggered Yugoslavia's violent dissolution.

sub_clusters.name: Titoist Serbia & Provincial Autonomies
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's position in the Yugoslav federation, the 1974 Constitution granting extensive autonomy to Vojvodina and Kosovo, Belgrade as the federal capital, and the tensions this created.

sub_clusters.name: Milošević's Rise & Yugoslav Wars
sub_clusters.description: Milošević's 1987 'no one should dare to beat you' speech at Kosovo Polje, the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy (1989), the breakup of Yugoslavia, and the onset of the wars in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia.

960.name: Yugoslav Wars & NATO Bombing
960.description: Serbia (as Federal Republic of Yugoslavia) was embroiled in the wars in Bosnia and Croatia, international sanctions, the Kosovo War, and NATO's 78-day bombing campaign in 1999. Milošević's fall in October 2000 opened a new chapter.

sub_clusters.name: Bosnian War & International Sanctions
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's involvement in the Bosnian War, the Srebrenica genocide (1995), the Dayton Accords, and the devastating impact of international sanctions on Serbian society.

sub_clusters.name: Kosovo War & NATO Bombing (1999)
sub_clusters.description: The Kosovo Albanian insurgency, Serbian military operations, NATO's 78-day air campaign against Yugoslavia (March–June 1999), UN administration of Kosovo, and the 5 October 2000 revolution ousting Milošević.

960.name: Democratic Transition & EU Path
960.description: Post-Milošević Serbia pursued democratic reform and European integration. The assassination of Prime Minister Đinđić (2003), Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence (2008), and the balancing act between the EU and Russia define contemporary Serbia.

sub_clusters.name: Đinđić Assassination & Democratic Reforms
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's post-Milošević reforms, Đinđić's extradition of Milošević to The Hague, Đinđić's assassination (12 March 2003), Montenegro's separation (2006), and Kosovo's declaration of independence (2008).
key_events: Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić assassinated (12 March 2003)

sub_clusters.name: EU Candidacy & Geopolitical Balancing
sub_clusters.description: Serbia's EU candidate status (2012), the Belgrade-Pristina dialogue, President Vučić's balancing between EU integration and Russian/Chinese relations, and the unresolved Kosovo question.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
